sentences.text: Manidens is the sister taxon of the closely related South African dinosaur Pegomastax.
This relatively basal heterodontosaurid grew up to 60 to 75 centimeters long, making it smaller than later forms.
Its sacrum was made of six fully fused vertebrae supported by robust ribs and ossified tendons that likely stiffened its back.
Manidens possessed distinctive proatlases in its neck vertebrae, a feature first reported in heterodontosaurids that connected to the skull base.
Fossil remains include a probable toe bone from the fourth digit and a flattened wrist bone.
The holotype specimen MPEF-PV 3211 consists of a partial skeleton including a skull, lower jaw, axial column, left shoulder girdle, and pelvis.
Manidens had long toe bones capable of grasping, with a smaller hallux that could still grip, similar to tree-perching birds.
The generic name Manidens refers to the hand-shaped form of its posterior lower teeth.
It is the first known heterodontosaurid to show dental replacement in its caniniform teeth, which may have occurred at a different time than its cheek teeth.
The type species Manidens condorensis was described in the journal Naturwissenschaften in 2011.
Manidens was named by Diego Pol, Oliver Rauhut, and Marcos Becerra.
Manidens had high-crowned teeth adapted for a herbivorous diet but lacked the wear facets found in more advanced forms.
Manidens had high-crowned teeth indicating an adaptation to a herbivorous diet, though they lacked the worn facets seen in advanced forms like Heterodontosaurus.
Researchers speculate that Manidens may have been partially carnivorous based on its unusual tooth morphology.
Manidens exhibited asynchronous tooth replacement in a continuous anterior-to-posterior wave pattern.
Researchers suggest that Manidens may have possessed filamentous integumentary structures based on evidence from the related Tianyulong.
Filamentous integumentary structures found in the relative Tianyulong suggest that Manidens may also have possessed them.
Fossil evidence suggests Manidens may have been at least partially arboreal.
Manidens is classified in the family Heterodontosauridae.
Manidens is the sister taxon to a clade containing the African species Heterodontosaurus, Abrictosaurus, and Lycorhinus, indicating an early evolutionary radiation of heterodontosaurids.
Pol et al. regard the genus Echinodon as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.
Fossils of Manidens were found in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in Chubut Province, Argentina, and are dated to the Toarcian stage.
Manidens lived approximately 179 to 178 million years ago during the Middle-Late Toarcian.
Manidens lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately 171 to 167 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Manidens fossils were found in the Queso Rallado locality of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, dating to the Aalenian or early Bathonian, 171 ± 5 to 167 ± 4 million years ago.
The genus Manidens existed from the Toarcian to the Aalenian, between 184.2 and 170.9 million years ago.
Manidens fossils come from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, an environment with lacustrine and fluvial deposits that coevolved with volcanic activity.
